1.pericope_label: Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not. And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee? Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one. Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass; Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day.

schools.summary: Ellicott joins verse 1 to the close of the preceding chapter as one sentence, renders verse 4 as a wish rather than a question, and takes the hireling's day of verse 6 as rejoicing at payday; Delitzsch grounds the frailty of man in the weakness and ritual impurity attending his birth.
Gill uses the same distinction between the first man and his descendants to identify the speaker with Job himself rather than with humanity at large.

Clarke finds a wordplay on the two Adams in the Hebrew and denies that the appointed bounds of verse 5 are fixed for individuals rather than for the race, emptying the alchemists' claims along the way; Wesley holds the opposite, that a certain end is appointed beyond which no man can prolong his life.

Henry reads the whole passage as a doctrine of original sin and a fixed term, insisting that the bounds God has appointed cannot be passed and that we are governed neither by blind fate nor by blind fortune.
Gregory reads the two measures of verse 5 as opposed, the days short and ours, the months multiplied and with God, so that the counting of months itself promises a life extended afterwards.

debates: Whether the appointed bounds of verse 5 are fixed for each individual, as Henry, Wesley and Gregory hold, or only for the race in general, as Clarke argues from the fact that folly and wickedness shorten life.
Whether verse 4 is a rhetorical question about inherited corruption or, as Ellicott alone suggests, an unfulfilled wish.
Whether "accomplish" in verse 6 means finishing the day's labour or, as Ellicott renders it, taking pleasure in the day the wages are paid.
outliers: Clarke supports the fixed-term denial with a catalogue of alchemists who promised an elixir of life, noting that all of them are dead and that the ninety years credited to Artephius became nine hundred only when a disciple added a cipher.
themes: Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.
He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not.
And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee?
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.
Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;
Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day.

7.pericope_label: For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he? As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up: So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies there is any comparison in verse 11, the Hebrew having no particle of comparison and the sea never failing, and reads the relation as one of contrariety; he finds no hope of a future life in the passage, only an unexpressed longing glimmering through it. Delitzsch renders the verb of verse 10 in the neuter, the man lying stretched out and gone without a trace.

Gill checks the botany and concedes the cypress as a counterexample, holding that since the claim is true of some trees it is sufficient to Job's purpose; he also allows the rendering of verse 11 without the comparative particle.

Clarke argues from cuttings and the rose of Jericho that few trees fail to sprout again, reads verse 11 as the water cycle and so as a consolation about the continuance of the race, and denies that the passage can be twisted into a denial of the resurrection or into soul-sleep; Wesley keeps the simile of the dried-up river as plain irrecoverability.
Henry grades vegetable, animal and rational life, holding the last beyond recall by any power of nature, and takes the resurrection to have been an article of Job's creed.

debates: Whether few trees revive when cut down, as Clarke holds, or whether the cypress and its like are common enough to qualify the figure, as Gill allows.
Whether verse 11 is a comparison at all: Ellicott says the Hebrew has no particle and the sense is contrariety, Wesley keeps the simile, and Clarke turns it into the water cycle.
How much of the resurrection is in the passage: Henry finds it an article of Job's creed, Clarke says it cannot be denied from these words, and Ellicott finds no hope of it here at all.
outliers: Clarke quotes the ancient epitaph on Bion, in which garden herbs wake again while the great and the wise sleep the endless sleep, and calls it the most cold and comfortless philosophy ever invented.
themes: For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease.
Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground;
Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant.
But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?
As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up:
So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep.

13.pericope_label: O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me! If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands. For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin? My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders "my change" as the transition from life to death, so that the hope is of being called and answering rather than of rising, yet concedes that the question of verse 14 would be pointless if the answer were certainly no; Delitzsch rejects the view that the sealed bag holds a verdict awaiting execution.

Gill takes the request to be hidden literally, canvassing the prophet's chambers, Hades and a cavern in the earth, and concluding that Job would rather be buried alive; he leaves verse 15 open between death and the resurrection and reads the sealed bag both ways.

Clarke divides verse 13 between body and spirit, takes "my change" as renovation and therefore of the resurrection, and construes the particle of verse 16 as concessive so that the complaint becomes a confidence; Wesley keeps the grave as a hiding-place and judges that Job here speaks rashly.
Henry allows that Job does right to the divine justice in owning his sins but wrong to the divine goodness in making God extreme to mark them, and declines to dwell on what was unadvisedly said.

debates: What "my change" means in verse 14: renovation and so the resurrection, as Clarke argues from the word used of grass springing again, or simply the passage from life to death, as Ellicott and Wesley take it.
Whether the sealed bag hides Job's transgression from himself, so that he cannot learn what he is punished for, or preserves it as evidence against him.
Whether verse 16 is a complaint at all, since Clarke construes its opening particle as concessive and turns it into an assurance of mercy where Henry and Wesley rebuke the speaker for rashness.
outliers: Clarke illustrates the sealed bag from the news of the day, noting that as he writes in July 1820 charges of state transgressions sealed in a green bag and laid before both houses of parliament are making a considerable noise in the land.
themes: O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me!
If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands.
For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin?
My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity.

18.pericope_label: And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place. The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth; and thou destroyest the hope of man. Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth: thou changest his countenance, and sendest him away. His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them. But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn.

schools.summary: Delitzsch shows the verb of verse 20 is transitive, seizing rather than prevailing, and denies that it refers to the sufferings of a lifetime; Ellicott reads verses 16 to 22 as one continuous complaint in which persistent persecution wears the speaker away as water wears rock.

Gill presses the finality of each image, the dissolved mountain never gathered up again and death reigning with despotic power, and hesitates over the last verse between the pains of the death-bed and the body rotting in the grave.

Clarke supplies the Latin and Greek forms of the proverb about constant dropping, suspects in the changed countenance the covering of a condemned man's face, and lays out five renderings of the last verse without settling among them, preferring the one that personifies flesh and breath as mourners; Wesley compresses the whole series of images into a single figure of irrecoverable loss.

Henry reads the decay of mountains and stones as proof that everything on earth is the worse for the wearing, distinguishes two causes for the changed countenance, and turns the dying man's ignorance of his children into counsel against anxious care for our families.

debates: What verse 22 describes: the pain of a dying man, the decay of the corpse, or the flesh and the breath personified as mourners over the body.
Whether the changed countenance of verse 20 is the alteration wrought by disease and fear, as Henry holds, or the veiling of a condemned man's face before execution, as Clarke suspects.
Whether the verb of verse 20 means that God proves stronger than man or that he seizes him, which Delitzsch argues against the older expositors.
outliers: Henry observes that while everything on this earth is worn away by time, it is not so with the heavenly bodies.
themes: And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place.
The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth; and thou destroyest the hope of man.
Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth: thou changest his countenance, and sendest him away.
His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them.
But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn.
